note: el (m), la (f), los (m. pl.), las (f. pl.). With an accent, “él” = he. a + el = al, de + el = del.
Plural: las (las casas).

examples: I have a dog and two cats.
note: un (m), una (f); unos, unas = some, a few.
The pronoun is often left out; the verb shows the person by itself: soy = I am.
Without an accent = your; with one, “tú” = you. Plural: tus (tus hermanos).
With an accent = you; without one, “tu” = your.
With an accent = he; without one, “el” = the.
The polite way to address one person; the verb goes in the 3rd person: usted habla = you speak.
A group of women only says “nosotras”.
ellas = they (women only).

examples: Do you all want something to drink?
note: In Mexico the only form for “you” to several people, friends and strangers alike. Vosotros isn't used.
Plural: mis (mis amigos). With an accent, “mí” = me (para mí = for me).
The context tells which: his / her / your (usted, ustedes) / their. Plural: sus.
nuestra, nuestros, nuestras, to match the noun.
esta (f), estos, estas. Careful: esta = this, está = is.
esa (f), esos, esas.

examples: Do you want something to drink?

note: The double negative is correct in Spanish: no… nada = nothing.

examples: I think it's going to rain.
The car that I bought is red.
note: Without an accent = that / which; with one, “qué” = what.

examples: What do you want to eat?
note: Always with an accent in questions and exclamations.
Plural: quiénes (¿Quiénes vienen?).
¿Cuál es…? asks you to pick from possibilities (a name, a number, an address); ¿Qué es…? asks for a definition.
¿Adónde vas? = Where are you going?
Without an accent, “como” = like, as, or “I eat” (comer).
The answer: porque (one word, no accent) = because.

examples: I'm not going because I'm tired.
The keys are on the table.

note: de + el = del (la casa del vecino). Spanish has no 's: el carro de mi papá = my dad's car.
a + el = al. Before a person who is the object: Veo a mi mamá = I see my mom.
conmigo = with me, contigo = with you.

examples: A coffee with no sugar, please.
I study in order to learn.
The store is open until nine.
The bank is between the pharmacy and the hotel.
Your phone is on the bed.
The cat is under the bed.
I want tacos and a water.
note: Before a word that starts with i-/hi- it becomes “e”: padre e hijo.

examples: It's expensive, but it's very good.
If it rains, we're not going.
I don't know if he's coming.
note: Without an accent = if / whether; with one, “sí” = yes.
muy + adjective (muy bueno), mucho + verb or noun (trabajo mucho).

examples: I have a lot of friends.
note: Before a noun it changes: mucha agua, muchos amigos, muchas gracias.
un poco = a little; poco = not much (como poco = I don't eat much).
In Mexico also “really”: bien bonito = really pretty.
Always with an accent. más… que = more… than.
As an adjective = alone (a woman says: vivo sola).

examples: I almost always eat at home.

note: Before a masculine noun: buen (un buen día). In Mexico people answer the phone with “¿Bueno?” = Hello?
Before a masculine noun: mal (un mal día).
Never “un otro”: otro café = another coffee.
As an adjective: todo el día, toda la noche, todos los días, todas las semanas.

examples: Every day I learn something new.
note: It never changes: cada día, cada semana.

examples: It's expensive; however, it's worth it.
It's pretty and, besides, it's cheap.
Even though it's raining, we're going out.
While I cook, I listen to music.
I'm tired, that's why I'm staying home.
I drink coffee; my wife, on the other hand, prefers tea.
In the end we didn't go.
I like Mexican food, especially tacos.

note: Very common in Mexico, also as a filler word.

examples: I arrive on Monday, that is, in three days.
Since you're here, help me with this.
We went out despite the rain.

note: Before a noun: cualquier; on its own: cualquiera.

examples: Someday I'm going to live in Mexico.
note: Before a masculine noun: algún.
Before a masculine noun: ningún. Used with a negative: no… ningún.

examples: He didn't study; therefore, he failed.
It was raining, but we went out anyway.
Instead of going to the movies, we stayed home.
He was tired; even so, he finished the job.
